screens.title: Candidate versus Active Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Start by making the distinction clear: the candidate configuration is your working draft in configuration mode, and the active configuration is the live state the device uses to forward traffic and run services. When you make changes in configuration mode, those edits alter the candidate configuration only. Nothing on the wire changes until you run commit, which validates and applies the candidate into the active configuration. A concrete example is adding a system description. If you set the description in config mode but do not commit, the router will not advertise or show that description when queried from operational mode. A common misconception is to assume edits are live immediately; this causes confusion when multiple administrators are working concurrently. Another confusion is thinking commit automatically saves a file to disk beyond what Junos stores in its commit history. Junos saves the previous committed versions automatically, but your explicit file backups still matter. Key takeaway: treat candidate edits as drafts—use show compare to validate differences, then commit when you are sure. A short check: if you want to discard uncommitted edits, use rollback without a number to return the candidate to match the active configuration. How would you verify your draft before committing?

keyIdea.title: Draft vs live
keyIdea.text: Candidate edits are safe until committed; commit makes them active. Use compare and rollback to control risk.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Candidate vs Active Configuration
Definition
Candidate configuration
Working draft stored while you are in configuration mode. Changes here are not active until you commit.
Active configuration
The running configuration that controls interfaces, routing, and services on the device.
Misconception
Editing in config mode does not change the running device until commit is issued. Never assume an uncommitted edit is live.
Concrete example
You add a system description in configuration mode, then run show | compare to confirm. The description appears in candidate only until you commit.
Procedure checklist
  • Enter configuration mode.
  • Make edits and run show | compare to inspect differences.
  • Commit to move candidate to active, or rollback to discard edits.
Key Takeaway

Think in two states: draft and live. Use compare and rollback to validate and protect running services.

screens.title: Viewing Configurations: Hierarchical and Set Output
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing how to view configurations in both the hierarchical tree and flat set-style is a practical tool. The hierarchical display shows the nested structure that is easiest to read when you want context, while the set-style output shows each statement as a separate command, which is easier to copy into scripts or selective loads. For example, run show configuration piped to display set to generate reusable set commands that recreate the same settings. Another useful pattern is running show from inside configuration mode to see your candidate view. When you are preparing a file to load, using display set helps you extract only the statements you need. A common mistake is to assume set-style output preserves comments or ordering; it flattens the structure into independent statements and may reorder items. Always verify critical dependencies after reconstructing a config from set statements. Practice by exporting a small interface section in set style, then reloading it with load merge to confirm it applies correctly. A good closing question: when would you prefer hierarchical output over set-style when troubleshooting? Viewing Configurations: Hierarchical and Set Output means hierarchical for human context; set-style for scripting and partial replacement via load commands.. In practical terms, use show configuration and display set for readable and scriptable output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Viewing Configurations
Hierarchy view
The hierarchical output shows nested braces and structure, making it easy to see parent-child relationships such as protocols, interfaces, and routing policy sequences.
Use when you need to understand context and related settings before changing anything critical.
Set-style output (flat)
# show configuration | display set
set system host-name MyJunosRouter-v2
set interfaces ge-0/0/0 unit 0 family inet address 192.0.2.1/24
set system services ssh root-login deny
Set-style is ideal for copying lines into a file for load merge or scripting. It flattens nested blocks into individual commands.
Common Mistake

Do not assume set-style preserves comments or original order; it is a reconstruction useful for automation but not a perfect round-trip for human annotations.

screens.title: Compare Candidate and Active Configurations
screens.narratorSegment: Before committing any edit, you should inspect what changed. The compare command highlights additions and deletions between the candidate and the active configuration. Use show followed by pipe compare while in configuration mode to list differences with plus and minus markers. This gives you a clear checklist of what will change when you commit. A concrete example is changing a hostname: after you set the new hostname in the candidate, run show pipe compare to see plus for the new set line and minus for the old one. A common misconception is that compare is only useful for big changes; in fact small deletions can be more harmful, especially when an unintended minus removes an essential setting. Your process should be: make edits, run show compare, review any removals, and only then commit. If you spot an unwanted deletion, either fix the candidate or discard uncommitted edits with rollback. Key takeaway: compare is your last chance to catch deletions and to confirm additions before they affect live traffic. Compare Candidate and Active Configurations means use compare to catch deletions and unintended changes. it is the final verification step before applying edits.. In practical terms, using show compare to validate edits before commit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Review before commit
keyIdea.text: Use compare to catch deletions and unintended changes. It is the final verification step before applying edits.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Compare Configurations
How compare works
The compare output shows lines prefixed with plus for additions and minus for deletions. It reports changes in set-style form so you can see exact statements affected.
Always scan for minus lines. A deletion might remove a service, ACL, or route policy that you did not intend to touch.
Example snippet
# show | compare
- set system services telnet
+ set system services ssh
This shows telnet will be removed and ssh added. Confirm this change matches your intent before commit.
Key Takeaway

Make compare your standard pre-commit check to prevent accidental removals and service disruptions.

screens.title: Saving and Loading Configurations
screens.narratorSegment: Persisting and reusing configuration files is a routine task. You can save the active configuration to a file for archival or transfer using save followed by a filename, which stores it to a device path. This is important before major changes: keep a known-good copy. Loading lets you bring file contents into the candidate configuration using load with different options. The typical workflow is to save a working config, make changes in candidate, and if you need to reuse or apply a prepared file, run load merge, load override, or load replace depending on scope. A common mistake is saving files to a temporary location and not confirming their path; always verify the file exists and that you are loading the intended file. Also, remember that saving does not commit by itself—the saved file is a copy of the active state at that moment. Key takeaway: save often and use load modes intentionally to avoid accidental removal of settings. Saving and Loading Configurations means save a copy of the active config before risky edits so you can restore or reference it later.. In practical terms, save copies, then load files with the right mode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Save & Load
Saving the active configuration
Use save <filename> from operational mode to capture the current running configuration to a path on the device. This is handy before complex changes, and when you want to move config to another device.
Always confirm the save path and file name so you do not overwrite a valuable backup.
Loading files into candidate
Use load <filename> variants to bring file contents into the candidate configuration. Choose the mode carefully: merge adds or updates parts, override replaces everything, replace uses tags to swap sections selectively.
Key Takeaway

Files are a durable safety net. Save before change and verify loads in a candidate before committing.

screens.title: Load Modes: merge, override, replace
screens.narratorSegment: Loading configuration files is powerful but also where mistakes happen. There are three primary load options you should understand. Load merge combines the file with the existing candidate configuration; it adds new statements and the file's settings override duplicates. This is the safest general-purpose option when you want to add or update only parts of the config. Load override replaces the entire candidate configuration with the file contents; anything not present in the file will be removed, so use override when you intend a full configuration rebuild. Load replace sits between merge and override: it honors replace markers inside the file so only sections tagged for replacement overwrite corresponding candidate sections, while other sections are merged. A common error is running load override when merge was intended, which can erase sections and cause outages. Before loading any file, run show configuration on the candidate and compare it to the file's intended changes. Practice loading small snippets with merge first, then reserve override for known-good full configs. Which mode would you pick when adding a new BGP neighbor without touching other settings?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Load Modes
load merge
Merges file with candidate. Adds new statements and lets file override existing conflicting statements. Use for incremental updates.
load override
Replaces the entire candidate with the file content. Use only when you intend a full configuration replacement.
load replace
Replaces sections marked with replace tags, while merging other sections. Use when only specific blocks need swapping.
Practical checklist
  • Inspect the file contents before loading.
  • Use load merge for adding a neighbor or interface changes without touching unrelated settings.
  • Reserve load override for intended full rebuilds and verify backups first.
Common Mistake

Running load override unintentionally removes unlisted configuration elements. Always back up before override.

screens.title: Rollback: Commit History and Reverting
screens.narratorSegment: Rollback is one of Junos OS's strongest safety features. Each successful commit saves the previous active configuration so you can return to a prior state. By default Junos keeps the last fifty commits. Use show system commit from operational mode to list these saved points with a brief summary and timestamps. When you need to revert, enter configuration mode and issue rollback with an index number; rollback 0 restores the immediately preceding configuration, rollback 1 restores the one before that, and so on. If you have uncommitted edits you want to abandon, running rollback without a number reverts the candidate configuration to match the current active configuration. A typical workflow is to commit a change, discover an issue, and then rollback 0 followed by commit to make the rollback active. A misconception is believing rollback itself applies the config immediately without a commit; you still commit the rollback to make it the new active configuration. Practice by making small commits, viewing the commit list, and then using rollback N to validate the expected state restoration. What would you check after a rollback to confirm services are restored?

keyIdea.title: Fast recovery
keyIdea.text: Use show system commit to inspect history and rollback N to restore a tested, previous active configuration.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Rollback & Commit History
Inspect saved commits
# show system commit
commit 0: 2026-09-25 10:05:12 by user
commit 1: 2026-09-24 16:12:03 by admin
commit 2: 2026-09-23 09:00:00 by auto-backup
The list helps you choose which prior configuration to restore.
Rollback procedure
  1. Enter configuration mode.
  2. Run rollback N to load the desired prior configuration into candidate.
  3. Review with show | compare and then commit to make it active.
Key Takeaway

Rollback gives a fast, reliable way to return to a previous known-good state; always verify services after committing the rollback.

screens.title: Rollback vs Discarding Uncommitted Changes
screens.narratorSegment: It’s important to distinguish rolling back to a previous commit from discarding uncommitted edits. Rolling back to a numbered commit loads a previously committed configuration into the candidate; after review you commit the rollback to make it active. Discarding uncommitted changes is done with rollback without a number while in configuration mode — this resets the candidate to match the current active configuration and drops any edits you made since the last commit. A concrete scenario: you edit multiple settings for testing, realize the changes are wrong, and want to abandon them — use rollback alone to discard. If instead you committed a change and later detect a fault, use rollback 0 to restore the prior committed state. A misconception is thinking rollback without a number affects saved commit history; it does not. It only reverts the candidate. Key takeaway: use plain rollback to abandon drafts and numbered rollback to recover published states. After either action, always validate with operational show commands. Rollback vs Discarding Uncommitted Changes means rollback without a number discards uncommitted edits; rollback n restores a previous committed state to candidate for re-commit.. In practical terms, two different recovery actions with different scopes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two kinds of rollback
keyIdea.text: Rollback without a number discards uncommitted edits; rollback N restores a previous committed state to candidate for re-commit.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Rollback Types
Discard uncommitted edits
While in configuration mode, run rollback with no number to abandon any uncommitted changes and restore the candidate to the active configuration.
This is a local undo of the draft, not a restoration from history.
Restore previous commit
Use rollback N to load a prior committed configuration into the candidate. After review, commit to apply it live.
This is the mechanism for recovering from a bad committed change.
Key Takeaway

Use rollback without a number to cancel drafts, and numbered rollback when you need to restore an earlier published state. Validate services after either action.

screens.title: commit confirmed: Safe Remote Changes
screens.narratorSegment: Commit confirmed is a safety pattern for changes that could disrupt management access or critical services. When you issue commit confirmed, Junos applies the candidate changes but starts a timer — by default ten minutes. If you do not run a regular commit or otherwise confirm before the timer expires, the system automatically rolls back to the previous configuration. This prevents you from locking yourself out of a remote router after a risky change. A concrete example: you change an interface or a firewall rule remotely and use commit confirmed; if your session drops or the change breaks connectivity, the device will restore the previous configuration automatically. A common mistake is forgetting to confirm a commit confirmed change intentionally; this leaves the device to auto-rollback, which may be surprising if you wanted the change to persist. Workflow: make the change, run commit confirmed, test connectivity, and then run commit to finalize within the timer window. Key takeaway: use commit confirmed for any change that might affect your ability to access the device and always monitor the timer. commit confirmed: Safe Remote Changes means commit confirmed applies changes temporarily and automatically reverts unless you confirm, protecting remote sessions.. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › commit confirmed
How it protects you
commit confirmed applies changes but sets a countdown. If you cannot confirm the change before the timer ends, the device automatically reverts to the prior configuration, preventing long outages or loss of access.
Use this pattern for remote edits that could disable SSH, routing, or critical interfaces.
Workflow
  1. Make the risky change in candidate mode.
  2. Run commit confirmed to apply with a timer.
  3. Test connectivity; if OK, run commit to finalize before the timer expires.
Common Mistake

Forgetting to confirm leaves the change temporary and triggers an automatic rollback later. Always finalize intentionally when tests pass.

screens.title: Walkthrough: Make Changes, Commit, and Rollback
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a short lab sequence that ties the previous concepts together. Start in operational mode and enter configuration mode. Make a harmless initial edit such as changing the system description and commit it so you have a new saved point. Next, update the host-name and commit again; these commits create entries you can inspect with show system commit. Now attempt a potentially disruptive interface change and apply it with commit confirmed so you have an automatic safety net. Wait briefly to simulate testing, then choose to rollback to the previous commit with rollback 0 and commit the rollback to make it live. Throughout this process use show configuration pipe display set to capture set-style statements for reuse, and use show pipe compare after edits to verify additions and deletions. A common learner error is skipping compare and then being surprised by removals; make compare a habit. After the rollback, validate with operational show commands to ensure the hostname and interface state match the intended stable configuration. What did this sequence teach you about the balance between making changes and maintaining recoverability?

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: In practice, operators commonly make a few repeatable mistakes when managing Junos configurations. One is using load override when they intended to merge, which can remove unrelated configuration and cause outages. To avoid this, always preview the file and run a dry review of the differences after loading into candidate mode. Another mistake is skipping show | compare before commit; without that check you may inadvertently delete a setting. Make compare a required pre-commit step. A third error is forgetting to finalize a commit confirmed change; this leaves the change temporary and can lead to surprise rollbacks later. Always set a timer reminder or confirm immediately after testing. Finally, relying solely on saved files without using show system commit can lead to confusion over which committed state is current. Takeaway: build a short checklist—save, load into candidate, compare, commit or commit confirmed, test, confirm or rollback—and make it standard practice. Consequence: unintended removal of unrelated config. Prevention: preview the file and use merge for partial changes.
Mistake: Skipping compare

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the essential ideas to carry forward. First, candidate configuration is your working draft and active configuration is what the device runs; commit moves changes from draft to live. Second, use show configuration in hierarchical form for context and show piped to display set for flat, script-friendly statements. Third, run show | compare to inspect plus and minus lines and catch deletions before committing. Fourth, load merge, override, and replace are distinct: merge is for partial updates, override replaces the entire candidate, and replace allows targeted section swaps. Fifth, Junos keeps committed history accessible via show system commit, and rollback N restores earlier states. Finally, commit confirmed lets you apply a risky change with a timer-based automatic rollback if you cannot confirm. Keep these core concepts as your operational guardrails so you can change configs confidently and recover quickly when needed.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a practical understanding of how Junos OS manages configuration changes, how to apply new settings safely, and how to recover when something goes wrong. You will learn the difference between the candidate configuration you edit and the active configuration the device runs. I will show how to view configuration trees in human and in command-friendly forms, how to stage changes, and how to inspect differences before committing. You will also see the three load modes — merge, override, and replace — and when to use each to avoid removing needed settings. Then we cover Junos rollback behavior and the safety pattern commit confirmed, which helps prevent accidental lockout during risky remote changes. As an example, we’ll walk through a small sequence: set a description, commit it, make a risky interface change with commit confirmed, and then revert safely if needed. By the end you will know how to keep backups, review diffs, apply partial or full config files, and recover confidently. Consider when you would prefer a merge over an override, and how commit confirmed changes your risk tolerance.

These objectives focus your hands-on skills and judgment with Junos configurations. First, you will distinguish the candidate configuration you edit from the active configuration the router runs, and explain how the commit command moves changes from draft to live. Second, you will list commands that let you view configuration in hierarchical and flat forms, and use display set output to create reusable set-style statements. Third, you will apply the load command with merge, override, and replace options and choose the correct mode for adding partial changes, replacing an entire config, or replacing only marked sections. Fourth, you will perform rollbacks and use the commit confirmed safety pattern to avoid locking yourself out during risky remote changes. Each objective pairs a practical command pattern with why it matters, so you not only can run the commands but also select them correctly under real operational risk.

This second objectives slide drills into the judgement calls you'll make when operating Junos. You will practice using the show configuration command both in hierarchical form and in flat set-style output, because set-style is often easier when scripting or constructing partial files. You will routinely run show pipe display set to produce set statements for reproducible snippets. You will also learn to read show pipe compare output to see additions and deletions before committing, reducing surprises. For file operations, you will choose load merge to add or update parts without disturbing other config, load override when you intentionally replace everything, and load replace when you need targeted replacements using replace tags. Finally, you will use show system commit to inspect past commits and rollback commands to restore a previous known-good state. These competencies reduce operational risk and make change reversible; your milestone is confidently reverting a recent change and explaining why you chose merge or override.

Start by making the distinction clear: the candidate configuration is your working draft in configuration mode, and the active configuration is the live state the device uses to forward traffic and run services. When you make changes in configuration mode, those edits alter the candidate configuration only. Nothing on the wire changes until you run commit, which validates and applies the candidate into the active configuration. A concrete example is adding a system description. If you set the description in config mode but do not commit, the router will not advertise or show that description when queried from operational mode. A common misconception is to assume edits are live immediately; this causes confusion when multiple administrators are working concurrently. Another confusion is thinking commit automatically saves a file to disk beyond what Junos stores in its commit history. Junos saves the previous committed versions automatically, but your explicit file backups still matter. Key takeaway: treat candidate edits as drafts—use show compare to validate differences, then commit when you are sure. A short check: if you want to discard uncommitted edits, use rollback without a number to return the candidate to match the active configuration. How would you verify your draft before committing?

Knowing how to view configurations in both the hierarchical tree and flat set-style is a practical tool. The hierarchical display shows the nested structure that is easiest to read when you want context, while the set-style output shows each statement as a separate command, which is easier to copy into scripts or selective loads. For example, run show configuration piped to display set to generate reusable set commands that recreate the same settings. Another useful pattern is running show from inside configuration mode to see your candidate view. When you are preparing a file to load, using display set helps you extract only the statements you need. A common mistake is to assume set-style output preserves comments or ordering; it flattens the structure into independent statements and may reorder items. Always verify critical dependencies after reconstructing a config from set statements. Practice by exporting a small interface section in set style, then reloading it with load merge to confirm it applies correctly. A good closing question: when would you prefer hierarchical output over set-style when troubleshooting? Viewing Configurations: Hierarchical and Set Output means hierarchical for human context; set-style for scripting and partial replacement via load commands.. In practical terms, use show configuration and display set for readable and scriptable output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Before committing any edit, you should inspect what changed. The compare command highlights additions and deletions between the candidate and the active configuration. Use show followed by pipe compare while in configuration mode to list differences with plus and minus markers. This gives you a clear checklist of what will change when you commit. A concrete example is changing a hostname: after you set the new hostname in the candidate, run show pipe compare to see plus for the new set line and minus for the old one. A common misconception is that compare is only useful for big changes; in fact small deletions can be more harmful, especially when an unintended minus removes an essential setting. Your process should be: make edits, run show compare, review any removals, and only then commit. If you spot an unwanted deletion, either fix the candidate or discard uncommitted edits with rollback. Key takeaway: compare is your last chance to catch deletions and to confirm additions before they affect live traffic. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Persisting and reusing configuration files is a routine task. You can save the active configuration to a file for archival or transfer using save followed by a filename, which stores it to a device path. This is important before major changes: keep a known-good copy. Loading lets you bring file contents into the candidate configuration using load with different options. The typical workflow is to save a working config, make changes in candidate, and if you need to reuse or apply a prepared file, run load merge, load override, or load replace depending on scope. A common mistake is saving files to a temporary location and not confirming their path; always verify the file exists and that you are loading the intended file. Also, remember that saving does not commit by itself—the saved file is a copy of the active state at that moment. Key takeaway: save often and use load modes intentionally to avoid accidental removal of settings. Saving and Loading Configurations means save a copy of the active config before risky edits so you can restore or reference it later.. In practical terms, save copies, then load files with the right mode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Loading configuration files is powerful but also where mistakes happen. There are three primary load options you should understand. Load merge combines the file with the existing candidate configuration; it adds new statements and the file's settings override duplicates. This is the safest general-purpose option when you want to add or update only parts of the config. Load override replaces the entire candidate configuration with the file contents; anything not present in the file will be removed, so use override when you intend a full configuration rebuild. Load replace sits between merge and override: it honors replace markers inside the file so only sections tagged for replacement overwrite corresponding candidate sections, while other sections are merged. A common error is running load override when merge was intended, which can erase sections and cause outages. Before loading any file, run show configuration on the candidate and compare it to the file's intended changes. Practice loading small snippets with merge first, then reserve override for known-good full configs. Which mode would you pick when adding a new BGP neighbor without touching other settings?

Rollback is one of Junos OS's strongest safety features. Each successful commit saves the previous active configuration so you can return to a prior state. By default Junos keeps the last fifty commits. Use show system commit from operational mode to list these saved points with a brief summary and timestamps. When you need to revert, enter configuration mode and issue rollback with an index number; rollback 0 restores the immediately preceding configuration, rollback 1 restores the one before that, and so on. If you have uncommitted edits you want to abandon, running rollback without a number reverts the candidate configuration to match the current active configuration. A typical workflow is to commit a change, discover an issue, and then rollback 0 followed by commit to make the rollback active. A misconception is believing rollback itself applies the config immediately without a commit; you still commit the rollback to make it the new active configuration. Practice by making small commits, viewing the commit list, and then using rollback N to validate the expected state restoration. What would you check after a rollback to confirm services are restored?

It’s important to distinguish rolling back to a previous commit from discarding uncommitted edits. Rolling back to a numbered commit loads a previously committed configuration into the candidate; after review you commit the rollback to make it active. Discarding uncommitted changes is done with rollback without a number while in configuration mode — this resets the candidate to match the current active configuration and drops any edits you made since the last commit. A concrete scenario: you edit multiple settings for testing, realize the changes are wrong, and want to abandon them — use rollback alone to discard. If instead you committed a change and later detect a fault, use rollback 0 to restore the prior committed state. A misconception is thinking rollback without a number affects saved commit history; it does not. It only reverts the candidate. Key takeaway: use plain rollback to abandon drafts and numbered rollback to recover published states. After either action, always validate with operational show commands. Rollback vs Discarding Uncommitted Changes means rollback without a number discards uncommitted edits; rollback n restores a previous committed state to candidate for re-commit.. In practical terms, two different recovery actions with different scopes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
